name: St John's Co-Cathedral
label: St John's Co-Cathedral
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23352829: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Saint John's Co-Cathedral' (105 m across).
notes: Baroque cathedral with Caravaggio's Beheading of St John.

text.description: St John's Co-Cathedral is a Catholic church in Valletta, built by the Order of St John between 1573 and 1578 and designed by the Maltese architect Girolamo Cassar. From the street it looks plain and almost fortress-like: a calm, well-proportioned stone façade with a bell tower at each side and an open balcony above the doorway, from which the Grand Master once addressed the crowds. That sober front is part of the fun, because the inside is a complete contrast. In the 1660s the artist Mattia Preti redecorated the interior in rich Baroque style, with carved stone walls and a painted vaulted ceiling showing scenes from the life of John the Baptist. The painted figures beside the columns are made to look like three-dimensional statues, so look closely. The marble floor is a patchwork of tombs, said to hold about 400 knights and officers of the Order. This is why the cathedral photographs so well: you get a strong, simple exterior and a golden, ornate interior in one stop. On the outside, stand back far enough to fit both bell towers and keep the vertical lines straight. Inside, work with the ceiling, the long view down the nave and the patterned floor. A phone copes well with all three if you hold it steady. Rules on photography inside can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: St John's Co-Cathedral stands in Valletta, Malta, where the Order of St John commissioned the cathedral after the Great Siege of 1565.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so head for Valletta by taxi or hired scooter and make for the cathedral in Valletta. Once you are inside Valletta, the cathedral is easy to find on foot, and the phone icon on the map sits right at the building. Check the official site before you go for entrance details. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the nave and ceiling, then switch to the default lens (1x) for the façade and for calmer, less stretched views. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it for carved details and ceiling figures.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the façade, walk out to the street or square outside and step back until both bell towers fit.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the two bell towers level with the lines so the façade does not lean. Inside, stand in the centre of the nave and aim along it for a symmetrical shot, or tilt up for the painted vault. Include a patch of the tomb-covered floor in the foreground for depth.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the scene to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the gold and carved stone keep their detail. Inside, brace your elbows against your body and hold still, as the light is dim and night mode may start up. Panorama can work outside but tends to bend the interior lines.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit early or late in the day, when it is often quieter, so you can shoot the interior without too many people in the frame.

text.access_note: This is a working church and a visitor attraction, so entry and photography rules may apply; check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The interior is fairly dim, so a phone may switch to night mode there.
Early or late in the day is often quieter.
Rules on photography inside the cathedral may change or be restricted.

name: Upper Barrakka Gardens
label: Upper Barrakka Gardens
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Upper Barrakka Gardens' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/561351027: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Upper Barrakka Gardens' (13 m across).
notes: Classic panorama of the Grand Harbour.

text.description: Upper Barrakka Gardens is a public garden on top of Saints Peter and Paul Bastion, built in the 1560s, and it stands at the highest point of Valletta's city walls. Most visitors head straight for the open terrace and its harbour view, but the quieter, more interesting pictures are in the colonnaded arcades at the end of the garden. The repeating stone arches make strong lines, and the Grand Harbour shows through the openings like a series of small framed pictures. The arches were built in 1661 by the Italian knight Fra Flaminio Balbiani. They were originally roofed, and the ceiling came off after the Rising of the Priests in 1775, which is why they are open to the sky today. Around you there are monuments to well-known figures, including Sir Winston Churchill, and a replica of the Les Gavroches statue. For a phone, the arcades are an easy subject: step into the line of arches, let them lead the eye towards the harbour, and keep the phone level so the columns stay straight. If you want the classic view instead, move out to the terrace and put the stone arches in the foreground, with the Grand Harbour and Fort St Angelo behind. The daily cannon firings at the Saluting Battery below usually draw a crowd to the terrace, so arrive early if you want a clear spot there.
text.geographic_location: In central Valletta, on the upper tier of Saints Peter and Paul Bastion, on the city wall above the Grand Harbour. The Saluting Battery is on the lower tier directly below.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the centre of Valletta and walk towards the Grand Harbour side of the city walls, where the gardens sit on the bastion. You can also arrive from the waterfront at Lascaris Wharf by the Barrakka Lift, which links up to the gardens. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to catch the full run of arches, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched frame. Use telephoto (2x or more) to pick out the harbour through a single arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the arches and arcade lines fill the frame, with the harbour glimpsed through the openings.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Place yourself in line with the arches so they lead the eye along the arcade and the harbour shows at the far end or through the gaps. Switch on gridlines to keep the columns upright. For a second option, step out onto the terrace and shoot back with the stone arches in the foreground and the Grand Harbour and Fort St Angelo behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the glowing harbour or the brightest arch to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the lit stone doesn't wash out. In dim light, hold the phone steady against a column and let night mode do its work.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After sunset, when the arcades are lit and the stone has a warm glow.

text.access_note: This is a public garden, so check the opening times on the official site before you go.

name: Fort St Elmo
label: Fort St Elmo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Upper Barrakka Gardens' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Upper Barrakka Gardens' (way/561351027): middle (13 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/7893491: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fort Saint Elmo' (247 m across).
notes: Star fort guarding the harbour entrance.

text.description:
Fort St Elmo is a star-shaped fort at the very tip of the Sciberras Peninsula, the narrow headland Valletta is built on. It sits between Grand Harbour and Marsamxett Harbour and guards the entrances to both. It is best known for the Great Siege of 1565, when its defenders held out for 28 days before it fell on 23 June. The delay gave the Knights time to prepare the other defences and wait for reinforcements. After the siege the ruined fort was rebuilt and made part of Valletta's new city walls. It was hit again in the Second World War, and the first air raid on Malta, on 11 June 1940, struck here. Restoration work finished in 2015.

The fort photographs well because of its shape. Sharp bastions and long, pale walls run out to the water, with open sea on one side and the Grand Harbour on the other. The classic view is from the upper terrace of Upper Barrakka Gardens, a free public garden. From there the whole fort sits at the harbour tip, set against the water and the Valletta waterfront. The fort is a fair distance away, so it will look small at the default lens (1x). Zoom in to pick it out, but keep some of the harbour in the frame, because the setting is what makes the shot. Lower Barrakka Gardens is a quieter place with a similar angle.
text.geographic_location: Fort St Elmo stands at the seaward tip of Valletta, where the Sciberras Peninsula ends between Grand Harbour and Marsamxett Harbour.
text.directions_text: Head for Upper Barrakka Gardens in Valletta. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to see how the fort sits in the harbour, then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the walls and bastions closer. Ultra-wide (0.5x) will make the fort look very small from here, so save it for the garden terrace itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Upper Barrakka Gardens (upper terrace, looking across the harbour). The whole Fort St Elmo at the harbour tip, framed against the Grand Harbour water and the Valletta waterfront. Looking across the harbour. From here the whole fort shows against the Grand Harbour water and the Valletta waterfront.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the fort on one of the lower thirds, with the water filling the rest of the frame. If you use zoom, keep a strip of the harbour and the waterfront in view so the fort still looks like it is at the end of the land. For a closer, wider view of the walls with open sea behind, you can try the fort's outer edge, but check the current access status first and expect wind there.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the fort to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and water keep their colour and the stone does not wash out. Wipe your lens before you start, as zoomed shots show smudges. At 3x or more, hold the phone with both hands and rest your elbows on the wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Try the afternoon, when the sun is likely behind you and lights the fort's walls. Early in the day the garden is likely to be quieter, but the low sun in front of you can make the fort look dark.

text.access_note: Upper Barrakka Gardens is a free public garden, but parts of Fort St Elmo itself may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

Early in the day the low sun may be in front of the viewer and make the fort look dark.

name: Fort St Angelo
label: Fort St Angelo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Upper Barrakka Gardens' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Upper Barrakka Gardens' (way/561351027): middle (13 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/54896162: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fort Saint Angelo' (356 m across).
notes: Fortress across the harbour in Birgu, seen from Valletta.

text.description: Fort St Angelo sits on the tip of Birgu, right in the middle of the Grand Harbour, so the best way to photograph it is from across the water in Valletta. From the terrace at Upper Barrakka Gardens you see the fort with Birgu and Senglea around it and the harbour stretching between you. The fort began as a medieval castle called Castrum Maris, the 'Castle by the Sea'. The Order of Saint John rebuilt it as a bastioned fort between the 1530s and the 1560s, and it was the Order's headquarters during the Great Siege of 1565. The layout you see today comes from a major rebuild in the 1690s, designed by Carlos de Grunenbergh. The British garrisoned the fort from 1800 to 1979, and it has been on Malta's tentative UNESCO World Heritage list since 1998. It works well on a phone because the shape is simple: pale bastion walls rising from the water, with the harbour as a natural foreground. Because the fort is across the harbour, it looks fairly small at the default lens (1x), so think of the shot as a wide harbour scene first and use the zoom for a closer, tighter picture. If you have time, the Saluting Battery gives a similar view from an old artillery platform above the water.
text.geographic_location: Fort St Angelo is in Birgu (Vittoriosa), at the centre of the Grand Harbour, across the water from Valletta rather than inside it. The photo is taken from the Valletta side, on the upper terrace of Upper Barrakka Gardens above the harbour.
text.directions_text: Upper Barrakka Gardens is on the Valletta side of the Grand Harbour, above the harbour. From the town centre, walk towards the harbour edge. The fort lies across the water to the south-east, so you photograph it from the terrace rather than walking to it. If you want to visit the fort itself, check the official site for how to get to Birgu. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole harbour scene, then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the fort closer. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of terrace or sky, as it will make the fort very small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Upper Barrakka Gardens (Valletta side, upper terrace above the Grand Harbour). Fort St Angelo across the harbour, with Birgu and Senglea around it and the Grand Harbour in the middle distance. Face south-east. From there you see Fort St Angelo across the water, with Birgu and Senglea around it and the harbour in the middle distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the fort a little off-centre and let the harbour water fill the foreground, with Birgu and Senglea either side. Switch on gridlines and keep the horizon level. For a different angle, try the Saluting Battery, which also shows the fort on the Birgu tip, or Gardjola Gardens, which shows Valletta's waterfront and domes with the fort in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the fort to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the stone keeps its colour. With telephoto, hold the phone steady against the terrace wall or rail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stonework. Check the light on the day, as it changes with the season.

text.access_note: Upper Barrakka Gardens is a free viewpoint, but the fort itself may be ticketed or have restricted areas, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: From Upper Barrakka Gardens the fort looks fairly small at the default lens (1x) because it is across the harbour.
Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stonework.

name: Grandmaster's Palace
label: Grandmaster's Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Misraħ San Ġorġ' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Misraħ San Ġorġ' (relation/8021724): middle (111 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/4434917: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Grandmaster's Palace' (178 m across).
notes: Former palace of the Knights, now the President's office.

text.description:
The Grandmaster's Palace is the largest palace in Valletta and fills an entire city block in the centre of the city. It was built between the 16th and 18th centuries for the Grand Master of the Knights Hospitaller, who ruled Malta from 1530 to 1798. Later it served as the British governor's residence and then as the seat of Parliament. Today it houses the Office of the President of Malta. The main façade is plain and austere, in the Mannerist style, with heavy corner stonework and a straight cornice along the roofline. It is not perfectly symmetrical, because the building was altered so many times. The two arched doorways with ornate balconies above them and the long, closed timber balconies wrapping the corners were added in the 18th century. All of this gives you strong lines and texture to work with.

The easiest place to take it all in is Misraħ San Ġorġ (St George's Square), in front of the palace. From the square you can fit the full frontage into one frame, with the clock tower and fountains in the foreground. Stand back, keep the phone level so the rooflines stay straight, and let the long wall fill the picture. If you want a second, closer picture, the palace's restored wooden balconies and carved stonework look good from street level on Triq ir-Repubblika, with the red phone box in the frame. Take your time: the square is a natural first photo stop on a walk through Valletta.
text.geographic_location: In the middle of Valletta, on Republic Street (Triq ir-Repubblika), facing St George's Square (Misraħ San Ġorġ) opposite the Main Guard. The palace fills the block bounded by Archbishop Street, Old Theatre Street and Merchants Street.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, tram or station stops listed nearby, so plan to reach St George's Square on foot, along Republic Street in the centre of Valletta. Walk along Republic Street and keep the long palace wall on your side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole frontage in from the square, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural, less stretched view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the balconies, doorways and carved stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Misraħ San Ġorġ (in front of the palace façade). The palace's full frontage across the square, with the clock tower and fountains in the foreground. In front of the palace façade. From here you can see the full frontage across the square, with the clock tower and fountains in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the cornice up with a horizontal line so the long façade does not tilt. Use the fountains as a foreground to add depth. If you want a closer, more detailed view, walk to Triq ir-Repubblika and frame the wooden balconies and stonework with the red phone box beside them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the palace wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its colour. If you are using the ultra-wide, keep the phone upright and don't tilt it, or the building's edges will lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the day if you want fewer people in the square, and take a few shots at different times if you are passing more than once.

text.access_note: The façade and the square are public to view from outside, but the State Rooms and Armoury inside are a museum run by Heritage Malta, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The square is likely to be quieter early in the day.
A bright sky can make stonework look darker, so lowering the exposure may help.
Keeping the phone level helps keep vertical lines straight on a long building.

name: Tritons' Fountain
label: Tritons' Fountain
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'City Gate bridge' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'City Gate' (pois); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/561356942: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Triton Fountain' (49 m across).
notes: Modern fountain with three bronze Tritons by the city gate.

text.description: Tritons' Fountain is a big, bold piece of 1950s design that greets you just outside Valletta's City Gate. Three bronze Tritons, sea figures from myth, hold up a wide circular basin about 5 metres across. Two sit and one kneels, so the group has a pleasing spiral shape. They stand on a seaweed base inside rings of water basins clad in 730 tons of travertine. The Tritons stand for Malta's link with the sea. The fountain was designed and built between 1952 and 1959 by the sculptor Vincent Apap and the draughtsman Victor Anastasi, and it is counted among Malta's most important Modernist landmarks. It was restored and reopened on 12 January 2018. It photographs well because the pale stone, dark bronze and moving water make strong shapes, and the old bastions give it a proper backdrop. Technically it sits in Floriana, just outside the gate, on the site of a 17th-century lunette that once guarded the entrance to Valletta. The best-known view is from the City Gate side, where the face of each Triton can be seen. For a phone shot, keep the whole round shape in the frame. The gate stays behind you when you shoot from that side. Wait a moment for people to move out of the way. The square is busy with traffic and walkers, so take a few frames rather than one.
text.geographic_location: The fountain stands just outside Valletta's City Gate, at the entrance to the old town. It is technically in Floriana, in a square beside the bus terminus and the bastions.
text.directions_text: Head to Valletta's City Gate. The fountain stands in the square just outside, next to the bus terminus. Walk slowly and take care around the buses and traffic. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the fountain in its square. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the full basin and the bastions in one frame. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the bronze Tritons.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on City Gate bridge. The fountain framed from the approach toward the City Gate, giving a composition with the gateway in view. From this side you see the faces of the Tritons.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the basin near the centre of the frame. Keep the camera level, because the circular basin shows any tilt. For a close view of the three Tritons holding up the basin, with the City Gate behind them, try Triton Square as an alternative. If a fence gets in the way, use the telephoto lens (2x or more) rather than leaning in.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bronze figures to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pale travertine does not wash out. Try a Live Photo to catch the moving water, and hold still for a second.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early evening, once the fountain lights come on. Use night mode if the light fades, and keep your arms tucked in for steadiness.

text.access_note: This is an open public square beside the bus terminus, but check the official site before you go in case of works or restrictions.

name: Fort Manoel
label: Fort Manoel
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Triq ix-Xatt' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Triq ix-Xatt' (way/1358365004): point nearest the subject (323 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/551701982: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fort Manoel' (332 m across).
notes: Restored 18th-century fortress across Marsamxett Harbour.

text.description:
Fort Manoel is a square, four-bastioned star fort sitting low on Manoel Island, in the middle of Marsamxett Harbour. The Knights Hospitaller built it in the 18th century and named it after Grand Master António Manoel de Vilhena, who laid the first stone on 14 September 1723. It was meant to protect Valletta's flank from across the water. Later it served the British military until 1964, was badly damaged in the Second World War, and was restored in the early 21st century.

It photographs well from the water's edge because the pale limestone bastions form clean, angular lines against the sea, with Valletta's skyline stacked up behind. A good free viewpoint is the Gżira waterfront promenade (The Strand), looking across the water towards the bridge to the island. The fort's interior is usually closed apart from occasional open days, so plan on exterior photos only. The walk along the shore towards the island's bridge also gives you harbour views along the way.

If you are on the Sliema side instead, Tigné Pedestrian Bridge gives a direct view across the water to the fort. Hastings Gardens also gives a more distant harbour view, but check on the day before relying on it, because it looks towards the island rather than the fort itself. Keep the horizon level and let the water fill the lower part of the frame.
text.geographic_location: Fort Manoel stands on Manoel Island in Gżira, in Marsamxett Harbour, north-west of Valletta across the water. The Gżira promenade (The Strand) faces it from the shore.
text.directions_text: Public transport details are not given here, so simply head for the Gżira seafront. That is roughly 750 m in a straight line, which is an estimated 10–15 minute walk rather than a measured route. Cars are not allowed past the island entrance, so walk over the bridge from Gżira if you want to get closer. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole line of bastions with the water in front. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the walls and the Valletta skyline behind. The ultra-wide (0.5x) suits a close shot along the shore, but it makes the fort look small and distant.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Triq ix-Xatt (Gżira waterfront promenade (The Strand), toward the Manoel Island bridge). The fort's limestone bastions seen from the shore across the water, with Valletta's skyline behind. The first time you open the map, use that point as your starting position. If you want to get closer, walk along the promenade towards the bridge to Manoel Island, and stop where the fort sits clear of any boats or railings.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the waterline on the lower third, with the bastions along the middle line and Valletta's skyline above them. Keep the horizon level. Try one wide shot and one zoomed shot of the walls. For a different angle, Tigné Pedestrian Bridge on the Sliema side gives a direct view over the water to the fort.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pale stonework to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky keeps its colour and the walls do not wash out. Wipe your lens first, as sea air leaves a haze on it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour, when the low light warms the limestone walls and the Valletta skyline behind.

text.access_note: The promenade is a free public viewpoint, but the fort's interior is usually closed apart from occasional open days, so check the official site before you go if you want to visit inside.

name: Barrakka Lift
label: Barrakka Lift
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Upper Barrakka Gardens' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Upper Barrakka Gardens' (way/561351027): middle (13 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/2489082272: the OpenStreetMap point 'Barrakka Lift'.
notes: Lift between the Upper Barrakka and the Grand Harbour waterfront.

text.description: The Barrakka Lift is a modern lift that carries people between the Grand Harbour waterfront at Lascaris Wharf and the top of the bastion by the Upper Barrakka Gardens. It was opened in 2012 and stands about 58 metres tall. Its concrete shaft is wrapped in aluminium mesh, and the ride takes roughly 23 seconds. It replaced an earlier steel lift that ran from 1905 until 1973 and was pulled down in 1983. For photographs, the lift works best as a supporting subject rather than the main event. From the top of the gardens you can frame the upper end of the lift with the garden arcades around it and the harbour opening up behind. That gives a layered picture with a clear sense of place: old stone, a clean modern structure and open water. A second option is the foot of the lift, where the shaft climbs the bastion wall above the waterfront, with ferries nearby. A third is Pjazza Kastilja, which shows the gardens and the lift together in one frame from the city side. Keep verticals straight so the shaft does not lean, and include a bit of arcade or railing in the foreground for depth. Moving a few steps along the terrace changes how the arcades line up, so try two or three positions before you settle.
text.geographic_location: In the Valletta fortifications, in the ditch below St. Peter and Paul Bastion, right beside the Upper Barrakka Gardens. It runs down to Lascaris Wharf on the Grand Harbour side.
text.directions_text: There are no tram or railway stops listed for this spot, so head for the Upper Barrakka Gardens in Valletta. If you want the view from the waterfront, the lift also links Lascaris Wharf with the gardens above. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the arcades and harbour together, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner shot of the lift's upper end. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the mesh cladding, but not if it makes the frame too tight.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Upper Barrakka Gardens (the gardens' entrance and upper area near the lift's top station). The lift's upper end and the gardens' arcades framing the harbour view behind it. From here the lift lies about to the south, and your photo shows its upper end with the gardens' arcades framing the harbour view behind it. If you want the lift as the main subject, Pjazza Kastilja shows the gardens and the lift together from the city side.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the lift up with a vertical grid line so it stands straight. Put an arcade arch or a stretch of railing in the foreground to give depth, and leave the harbour as the background. For a different view, try the foot of the lift, with the shaft rising up the bastion wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the lift or the brightest part of the sky to set focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the exposure down a little, so the sky keeps its colour and the shaft does not go too dark. Hold the phone level to keep the lines straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or golden hour, as photo guides suggest for the gardens.

text.access_note: The gardens and the lift are public places, but access to the lift, including its hours and fares, can change, so check the official site before you go.

name: Lower Barrakka Gardens
label: Lower Barrakka Gardens
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Siege Bell War Memorial' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'World War II Siege Bell' (pois); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/27462446: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Lower Barracca Gardens' (115 m across).
notes: Quiet garden with the Siege Bell Memorial view.

text.description: The Lower Barrakka Gardens are a public garden in Valletta, twinned with the Upper Barrakka Gardens in the same city. They look out over the Grand Harbour and its breakwater, which gives you water and sky behind almost any frame. At the centre stands the Monument to Sir Alexander Ball, a neoclassical temple built in 1810 to honour Malta's first British Civil Commissioner. It is the most photogenic thing here: pale stone columns against shade trees and a harbour backdrop. The terrace also has several commemorative plaques, including ones for the 1956 Hungarian revolution, the Prague Spring and Giuseppe Garibaldi. The gardens and their arcades were extensively rebuilt in the 1980s and reopened in 2003 after a major rehabilitation project. For a quieter angle, start at the Siege Bell War Memorial, just outside the garden. Its bell monument makes a strong foreground, with the gardens and the harbour edge behind it. Then walk in and photograph the temple from the paths. Keep people in the frame for scale if you like, but wait a moment for a gap if the terrace is busy. If you want a closer, tidier view of the temple, stay on the paths and use the telephoto lens rather than stepping onto planted areas. Parts of the garden can be fenced off during works, so be ready to adjust your view.
text.geographic_location: In Valletta, on the Grand Harbour side of the city, twinned with the Upper Barrakka Gardens.
text.directions_text: No Underground, rail or tram stops are listed for this spot, so walk or use local transport in Valletta and head for the Lower Barrakka Gardens. Once there, go to the Siege Bell War Memorial, just outside the garden. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the bell monument with the gardens behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole garden and harbour edge, or the telephoto lens (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the temple.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Siege Bell War Memorial (just outside the garden's southern edge, looking back toward the gardens). The memorial's bell monument with the Lower Barrakka gardens and the harbour edge as a secondary backdrop. The photo shows the memorial's bell monument with the Lower Barrakka Gardens and the harbour edge as a secondary backdrop. The exact standing spot may vary a little, so adjust to get the bell monument and gardens in the same frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the bell monument in the foreground and let the garden and harbour edge sit behind it. Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon level. As a second option, walk into the garden and frame the Sir Alexander Ball monument between the shade trees and paths, with the harbour behind it in some frames.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the monument to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the stone and the harbour keep their detail. If you use ultra-wide (0.5x), keep important details away from the edges of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people, though the garden can be photographed at any time of day.

text.access_note: The Lower Barrakka Gardens are a public garden, but parts may be fenced off for works, so check the official site before you go.

name: Republic Street
label: Republic Street
camera_source: Commons cluster (6 photos), weak. Moved 53 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 85 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Main pedestrian street of the city.

text.description:
Republic Street is the main street of Valletta, running about 1 kilometre from City Gate towards Fort St. Elmo. The Order of St. John laid the city out on a grid after the Great Siege, and this street sits in the middle of that plan. It has carried several names over the years, including Strada San Giorgio, Strada Reale and Kingsway, before becoming Republic Street. It was heavily bombed in World War II. Today it is mostly pedestrianised, with only karozzini and electric cabs allowed to drive along it.

It photographs well because the grid layout gives you a long, straight street with side streets crossing it at right angles. Along the way you pass places such as the Parliament of Malta, the Royal Opera House, St. John's Square and Grandmaster's Palace, so there is always something to put in the frame. A karozzin passing through the shot adds a bit of local character.

For your phone, aim for a few different pictures rather than one. Take a wide view down the street, then move closer and zoom in on a doorway, a balcony or a shopfront. The street is busy at Christmas, so allow a little patience if you want a clear view.
text.geographic_location: Republic Street runs through the middle of Valletta, the capital of Malta, from City Gate at the landward end down towards the granaries at Fort St. Elmo. Many of the city's main buildings and squares are on or just off it.
text.directions_text: The street is mostly pedestrianised, so the last part is on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view down the street. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the buildings on both sides and plenty of sky. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as balconies and shop signs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in St George's Square (corner where the square meets the upper end of Republic Street). A panoramic view along the street from the square, with the Grand Master's Palace and the limestone facades framing the road. Keep to the side of the street so you are not in the way of people walking or a passing karozzin.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the street up with the centre of the frame so the buildings on both sides lead the eye into the distance. Keep the phone level so the tall buildings do not lean. For a second picture, zoom in on a single balcony or doorway. If a karozzin or electric cab comes by, wait for it to reach a clear spot in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the middle of the street to focus. Then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky looks washed out. If the street is lively, try a Live Photo and pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day is usually quieter, which gives you a clearer view along the street. It gets busy around Christmas, so expect more people then.

text.access_note: Republic Street is mostly pedestrianised and open to walk along, but some buildings on it may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The street is probably quieter early in the day than later on.
The long, straight street makes a good leading-line shot when you stand at one end.
Some buildings along the street may have ticketed or restricted entry.

name: City Gate
label: City Gate
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Triton Fountain' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Triton Fountain' (node/10056853582): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/33435233: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Valletta City Gate' (84 m across).
notes: Modern entrance by Renzo Piano.

text.description:
City Gate is the main entrance to Valletta, and the best-known way into the walled city. Its Maltese name is Bieb il-Belt, 'Door of the City'. The gate you see today is the fifth on this spot. It was designed by the Italian architect Renzo Piano and finished in 2014, and its modern lines contrast with the old fortification walls on either side. A bridge over the deep ditch leads up to it, and Republic Street, Valletta's main street, starts just beyond.

The first gate here dates from 1569, when it was called Porta San Giorgio. It has been rebuilt several times since, and the present gate is the fifth on the site.

For a phone photo, the classic view is from the Triton Fountain, in the pedestrian square just outside the gate. The three bronze Tritons and their basin fill the foreground, and the gate sits behind them like a frame. The fountain is lit at night, which many visitors find especially attractive. Early morning is calmer, with good light and very few people in the square.

If you want a second angle, go up to the gate itself and photograph the modern structure with the old walls on either side. Parliament House is close by, so look around before you leave.
text.geographic_location: At the entrance to Valletta, across the deep ditch, at the start of Republic Street. Parliament House and the City Gate Shopping Arcade stand close by.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stop is listed for this spot. Navigate to City Gate or the Triton Fountain and finish on foot. The square around the fountain is pedestrian. The gate is the point where Republic Street begins. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the fountain, the gate and some of the walls into one frame, then try the default lens (1x) for a tighter, tidier picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Triton Fountain (directly in front of the fountain, facing the City Gate). The three bronze Tritons and their basin in the foreground, with the City Gate and its entrance behind them. Do not shoot from the icon itself. Instead, walk to the Triton Fountain, just outside the gate, and stand directly in front of it facing the City Gate. From here the three bronze Tritons and their basin are in the foreground, with the gate and its entrance behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the fountain in the lower part of the frame, with the gate opening in the middle. Keep the phone level so the walls and the gate stay straight. For another view, walk up to the City Gate itself and photograph the modern gate with the old fortification walls on either side.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gate to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is bright. At night, use night mode and hold the phone as still as you can, resting your elbows on something solid.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before about 8:30, when the light is good and the square is nearly empty. The fountain is also attractive after dark, when it is lit.

text.access_note: The fountain stands in an open pedestrian square and the gate is the public entrance to the city, but check the official site before you go in case of works or closures.

name: Is-Suq tal-Belt
label: Valletta Market
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/31232775: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Valletta Food Market' (80 m across).
notes: Historic iron market hall, now a food hall.

text.description: Is-Suq tal-Belt is Valletta's covered market hall, built between 1859 and 1861 and now a busy food market with stalls and places to eat. It is a good stop for photos because the walls and arches are limestone, while the inside is bright and full of detail: slim iron columns, trusses and a timber-decked iron roof. It was the first building in Malta to be made mostly of prefabricated iron, and its design took ideas from Covent Garden in London and the Halles Centrales in Paris. The building was badly bombed in 1942 and lost about a third of its structure. It was later altered and then renovated in 2016-17, reopening to the public in January 2018. That mix of old iron frame and modern food stalls gives you plenty to point a phone at. Look for the long lines of the roof structure, the people at the counters and the colour of the food displays. Wide views of the hall work well, and so do close shots of a single stall or a plate of food. The building is about 80 metres across, so you can move around and try several angles. Indoor light is mixed and changes from one corner to another, so check each shot on screen before moving on. Be polite when photographing stallholders and other visitors, and ask first if you want a close portrait of someone.
text.geographic_location: Is-Suq tal-Belt is in Valletta, Malta. The earlier market building on the site had entrances to Merchants Street and St Paul's Street.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is listed for this spot. Plan your own route into Valletta and walk to the market. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the full length of the hall and its iron roof, then switch to the default lens (1x) for stalls and people. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as column tops, signs and food.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. You are standing in the middle of the building, so turn round slowly to find your angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the rows of iron columns with the vertical lines so the hall looks straight. Aim up for a shot of the roof structure, or hold the phone at chest height for a view down the aisle with people in it. For food, move in close with the default lens (1x) and tap the dish to focus.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the scene to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so windows and lights do not wash out. Use portrait mode for single dishes or drinks. Keep both hands steady, as indoor light can make shots blurry. Night mode may switch on by itself in dim corners, so hold still while it works.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go outside the busiest meal times if you want clear views of the hall without crowds. Daylight coming through the building helps the iron structure look its best.

text.access_note: The market hall is a public building with shops and places to eat, and opening times can change, so check the official site before you go.

name: Auberge de Castille
label: Auberge de Castille
camera_source: Commons cluster (23 photos). Moved 28 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 50 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/5760252: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Castille Place' (103 m across).
notes: Baroque building housing the Prime Minister's office.

text.description:
The Auberge de Castille is one of the grandest buildings in Valletta, and it sits at the city's highest point, looking out over Floriana and the Grand Harbour area. It was built in the Spanish Baroque style between 1741 and 1744 under Grand Master Manuel Pinto da Fonseca, replacing a 1570s auberge by Girolamo Cassar. It was originally a base for knights from Castile, León and Portugal. Today it houses the Office of the Prime Minister, and the name Castille is often used locally to mean the Prime Minister's office.

It photographs well because it is built to be looked at. The façade has eleven bays, ornate windows set in recessed panels, a strong cornice and rusticated corners. A flight of steps leads to the doorway, which is flanked by columns and topped by a bronze bust of Pinto and a trophy of arms. Two old cannons stand just in front of the entrance. The square in front is wide and open, so you can step back far enough to fit the whole front into one frame.

For a good phone picture, keep the phone icon on the map as your starting position and look north-east towards the building. Take one wide shot of the whole façade, then move in for details such as the doorway, the bust and the coats of arms. The building was restored between 2009 and 2014.
text.geographic_location: At Castille Place, at the highest point of Valletta. It stands close to Saint James Cavalier, the Malta Stock Exchange and the Upper Barrakka Gardens.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stops are listed for this spot, so start from the Upper Barrakka Gardens, which are close by, or travel to Castille Place in Valletta by taxi or hired scooter. Walk to the phone icon on the map. From there the middle of Castille Place is 49 m to the north-east, with the auberge on the square, roughly a minute on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 50 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole façade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you have to stand close, and use telephoto (2x-3x) for the doorway details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 50 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. You can step forwards or back from here to adjust your framing.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the cornice up with a horizontal line so the building does not lean. Keep the central steps and doorway in the middle of the frame and let the eleven bays spread out evenly to each side. Then zoom to 2x-3x for the bronze bust and the coats of arms above the door. For a different angle, try the ultra-wide lens from nearer the steps, tilting the phone as little as you can.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the pale stone looks washed out against the sky. Take a few shots, as passers-by often walk through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon, when softer, lower light brings out the carving on the stone.

text.access_note: The building is government offices, so expect to photograph it from the square outside; check the official site before you go if you hope to see anything more.

name: Collegiate Parish Church of St Paul's Shipwreck
label: St Paul's Shipwreck
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Triq San Pawl' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Triq San Pawl nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/33459935: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Church of Saint Paul's Shipwreck' (64 m across).
notes: Baroque church with a gilded interior.

text.description: The Collegiate Parish Church of St Paul's Shipwreck is a Roman Catholic parish church and one of Valletta's oldest. It honours St Paul, whose shipwreck on Malta is told in the Acts of the Apostles. The church goes back to the 1570s, was designed by Girolamo Cassar and was finished in December 1582. The tall, narrow facade you see today is later: it was rebuilt in 1885 to a design by Nicholas Zammit. The twin belfries and the Baroque front are what make it worth a photo. The church is squeezed between old stone buildings on a narrow street, so the picture is of a slim, richly detailed front framed by plain walls on either side. Inside are an altarpiece by Matteo Perez d'Aleccio and a wooden statue of St Paul carved in 1659 by Melchiorre Cafà. The statue is carried through Valletta's streets on the feast day, 10 February. The street is tight, so a clean, straight-on shot takes some care. Cross to the far side of the narrow street and step back as far as you comfortably can before you raise your phone. Keep the facade upright and wait for passers-by to clear the doorway. If you want a casual second angle, you could try Republic Street (Triq ir-Repubblika) and look down St Paul Street to see the front at an angle among its neighbours. Photography inside may be allowed for personal use except during services, so check on the day.
text.geographic_location: On St Paul Street (Triq San Pawl) in Valletta, wedged between the old stone buildings that line the narrow street.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot; walk in from the centre of Valletta and head for St Paul Street (Triq San Pawl). The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street feels too tight to fit the whole facade, then try the default lens (1x) from the far side. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the belfries and the carved detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Triq San Pawl (opposite the church facade, across the narrow street). The high, narrow Baroque facade and twin belfries of the church, framed by the street's old stone buildings. Opposite the church facade across the narrow street. From here the church is to the north-west, and you can see the high, narrow Baroque facade and twin belfries framed by the street's old stone buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Step back to the far side of the street to get the whole front in. Switch on gridlines and line the facade up with the vertical lines so the walls do not lean. Include a little of the neighbouring stonework on each side to show how closely the church is hemmed in. For a casual alternative, you could try Republic Street (Triq ir-Repubblika) and photograph the front at an angle down St Paul Street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then nudge the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. If you use the ultra-wide, keep the facade away from the edges of the frame to limit stretching.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight is easiest, when the facade is evenly lit. In a narrow street the light can change quickly, so check the screen and retake if one side is in deep shade. In the evening, try night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.

text.access_note: The church is a working parish church and a place of worship, so check the official site before you go for visiting times and photography rules inside.

sources.title: Collegiate Parish Church of St Paul's Shipwreck

name: Royal Opera House ruins
label: Royal Opera House
camera_source: Commons cluster (1 photos), weak. Moved 36 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 35 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/55064405: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Royal Opera House' (95 m across).
notes: Open-air theatre in the ruins of the bombed opera house.

text.description: The Royal Opera House ruins mark the spot where one of Valletta's most admired buildings once stood, just inside the city's entrance. Designed by the English architect Edward Middleton Barry, the theatre opened in 1866 and could seat 1,095 people, with room for another 200 standing. A fire gutted the interior in 1873, and it reopened in 1877 with Verdi's Aida. In April 1942 it was devastated by wartime bombing, and the remains were later cleared. The site then waited decades for a rebuilding plan. Today the Italian architect Renzo Piano's open-air design, opened in 2013 as Pjazza Teatru Rjal, occupies the site as an open-air theatre. It photographs well because the story is visible in the frame: old stone, open sky and a modern stage layout together. The mapped outline of the site is about 95 m across, so step back to take in as much as you can from a single spot. For the best result, look for any stonework or standing elements as your main subject and let the open space around them give the picture room. Keep the phone level using gridlines so any vertical lines do not lean. If people are walking through, wait a moment for a gap, or include one person to show the scale.
text.geographic_location: At the entrance to Valletta, near the City Gate and Freedom Square. It is on Republic Street, the street that was once called Strada Reale.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, rail or tram stops to give, so start from the City Gate and Freedom Square area at the entrance to Valletta, or arrive by taxi or hired scooter and ask for the Royal Opera House site (Pjazza Teatru Rjal). The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the open site in one frame, then try the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out details such as stone texture.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Pjazza Teatru Rjal (from the piazza, looking across the restored ruins toward the stage). The surviving columns of the old opera house standing against the modern stage and seating, with the city beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up any upright stonework or edges with the vertical lines. Keep some sky and some ground in the frame so the open, roofless nature of the site is clear. Move a few steps to the side if a lamp post or other object is crossing your subject.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. Use portrait mode only for a person standing in front of the stonework, not for the ruins on their own.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows on the stone. Midday sun can make the pale stone look flat and harsh.

text.access_note: This is a public city-centre site that is also used as a performance venue, so check the official site before you go in case an event limits access.
claims_not_in_sources: The site is at the entrance to the city near the City Gate and Freedom Square (the sources mention the city entrance, the city gate and Freedom Square).
Early morning or late afternoon light is usually softer on pale stone than midday sun.
The site may have limited access when performances or events are held.

name: National Library of Malta
label: National Library
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Misrah ir-Repubblika' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Misraħ ir-Repubblika' (way/31232942): middle (77 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/339474207: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'National Library' (56 m across).
notes: Neoclassical library on Republic Square.

text.description: The National Library of Malta, known locally as the Bibliotheca, stands on Republic Square in the middle of Valletta. It was founded in 1776 by Grand Master Emmanuel de Rohan-Polduc. The building was designed by the architect Stefano Ittar, and his son Sebastiano carried on the work after Stefano died. It was finished in 1796 but not opened until 1812, and it is an early example of neoclassical architecture in Malta. That helps your photo: the front is calm and symmetrical, with Doric and Ionic columns, an open loggia under the first floor and a balustraded balcony above the central doorway. The square gives you space to stand back and take it all in. The statue of Queen Victoria in the foreground, the trees and the café terraces make the picture feel like Valletta rather than a plain shot of a facade. The library is a Grade 1 national monument. Photography is not allowed inside, so keep your pictures to the outside. Republic Street is the city's busiest street, so expect people walking through your frame. Take a wide shot first, then move closer for the arches and the doorway behind them. Shooting through a gap between passers-by usually works better than waiting for the square to empty.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Valletta, on Republic Square (Misrah ir-Repubblika), close to the Grandmaster's Palace.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground, tram or train stop for this spot, so start from Valletta city centre and the Grandmaster's Palace area, or come by taxi or hired scooter and be dropped nearby. The library is to the south-east of it, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full facade with the statue in front. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you have to stand close and want to keep the whole front in the frame. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the arches and the doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Misrah ir-Repubblika (across the square from the main facade, with the Queen Victoria statue in the foreground). The neoclassical front of the library framed by the Queen Victoria statue and the square's trees and café terraces. Across the square from the main facade, with the Queen Victoria statue in the foreground. From here your photo shows the neoclassical front framed by the statue, the square's trees and the café terraces.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the columns up with the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean. Put the statue slightly off-centre, in the lower part of the frame, and let the facade fill the rest. For an alternative, walk closer in the square and take a tighter shot of the arcaded entrance. Or take a street-level view of the facade from Triq ir-Repubblika, the main shopping street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is washing out. This keeps the stonework looking rich rather than flat. Take two or three frames, because people keep walking through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the day or later in the afternoon if you want fewer people on Republic Street and in the square.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but check the official site before you go for the library's opening arrangements, and remember that photography is not allowed inside.

name: Church of Our Lady of Mount Carmel
label: Carmelite Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Tigné Point' (1 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Tigné Point Beach' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/33808113: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Basilica of Our Lady of Mount Carmel' (69 m across).
notes: Large dome that dominates the skyline.

text.description:
The Church of Our Lady of Mount Carmel is a Carmelite basilica whose big oval dome is one of the shapes that defines Valletta's skyline. The present building is quite young. It was built between 1958 and 1981, on the site of a late 16th-century church that was badly damaged by bombing in March 1942. The dome is about 42 m high and faces Marsamxett Harbour. It is reportedly designed to sit slightly higher than the bell tower of the nearby Anglican St Paul's Pro-Cathedral, so the two make a pairing in the same view.

The best way to photograph it is from across the water. The dome and the spire of St Paul's rise together above the rooftops, and the sandstone buildings below give the picture a warm, even base. Water in the foreground adds depth, and the sky behind the dome does much of the work. Blue hour suits it especially well.

On your phone, start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole skyline, then try a zoomed shot to bring the dome closer and fill the frame. Keep the dome and spire upright by using the gridlines, and keep the horizon level. If you would like a different angle, Upper Barrakka Gardens shows the dome from above with rooftops in front. Triq Zekka gives a street-level view, with the slope of the street leading your eye to the dome.
text.geographic_location: The church is in the middle of Valletta, in the old city, close to St Paul's Pro-Cathedral and facing the Marsamxett Harbour side. The viewpoint is across the water on the Sliema side, at Tigné Point.
text.directions_text: For this view, start from Sliema and head to Tigné Point on foot or by whatever local transport suits you; check a map for the route. The church is across the water to the south, so this is a viewing spot rather than a walk to the church. Once you are on the terrace, face south across Marsamxett Harbour and look for the dome and the spire beside it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole skyline, then use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the dome and spire closer. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of water and sky in the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Tigné Point (Sliema side, facing Valletta across Marsamxett Harbour). The church dome and St Paul's spire rising over the Valletta skyline, best with the blue-hour sky behind them. On the Sliema side, facing south across Marsamxett Harbour towards Valletta.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the dome and spire on one of the vertical lines, with the horizon level. Keep some water in the bottom of the frame for depth. For a different view, try Upper Barrakka Gardens (the dome from above, across the Grand Harbour) or Triq Zekka (a street-level view down the slope to the dome).
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the dome to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. When the light drops at blue hour, hold the phone steady against a rail or wall, or use night mode, and keep still while it takes the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: About one hour before sunset, when the low light warms the sandstone buildings. Stay on into blue hour for the sky behind the dome.

text.access_note: Tigné Point is an open terrace on the Sliema side; for the church itself, which is a place of worship, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Valletta lies roughly south of the Tigné Point viewpoint, so you face south for this view.
The dome and spire can be brought closer with a 2x-5x telephoto lens from across the harbour.
Holding the phone against a rail or wall helps keep it steady in low light.

name: Parliament House
label: Parliament House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pjazza San Ġorġ' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Każin Banda San Ġorġ' (way/329433684): middle (33 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/21084402: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Parliament House' (81 m across).
notes: Renzo Piano's limestone parliament building.

text.description: Parliament House is where Malta's parliament meets, and it is one of the most modern buildings in old Valletta. It was built between 2011 and 2015 to a design by the architect Renzo Piano, as part of the project to reshape the entrance to the city. It has two stone blocks joined by bridges, and the limestone slabs are carved so that they look eroded by nature. The stone came from Gozo, and the cladding was meant to suggest honeycombs. Locals have also likened it to a dovecote or a cheese grater, and it caused plenty of argument when it went up. That contrast with the old streets is why it photographs so well: strong shapes, repeating patterns and a lot of texture. It also stands out against the older buildings around it. The two blocks are kept apart so that views of Saint James Cavalier from Republic Street stay open. On a phone, this works best as two pictures: a wider shot that shows the building in its setting, and a closer one of the pattern in the stonework. The staircase and entrance are usually busy, so be patient and shoot between groups of people. Most of the building is closed to visitors, though a ground-floor exhibition is open to the public. Photography inside may be restricted, so keep your main pictures for outside.
text.geographic_location: Parliament House is at the entrance to Valletta, on Republic Street beside City Gate. It stands next to Saint James Cavalier and the ruins of the Royal Opera House, which is now an open-air theatre.
text.directions_text: The building lies to the north-west, about 30 minutes on foot. It is on Republic Street, beside City Gate, the main entrance to Valletta. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole building and its surroundings. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the staircase and cannot fit the front in. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details of the carved limestone.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Pjazza San Ġorġ (across the square from the building, or from its side). The Parliament building in its square, set against the historic Valletta streetscape and the Grand Master's Palace opposite. Stand in the open area near City Gate on Republic Street, facing the building from the side or at an angle rather than straight on. From here the photo shows Parliament House alongside Saint James Cavalier and the ruins of the Royal Opera House, with Palazzo Ferreria and the City Gate Shopping Arcade opposite.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the vertical lines of the facade parallel to the edges of the screen. Shooting from the side or at an angle gives more depth than a flat front view. For a second picture, go to the building itself and photograph the staircase and entrance facade, filling the frame with the stone-and-glass design. Wait for a gap in the crowd on the steps.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale limestone keeps its texture and does not wash out. Live Photos can help you pick a frame with fewer people in it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the day or later in the afternoon, when the stone has warmer, softer light and the staircase is usually quieter.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the public streets and squares, but most of the inside is closed to visitors and photography inside may be restricted, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The stone looks warmer in low morning or late-afternoon light.
The staircase is likely to be quieter early in the day or later in the afternoon.
The outside of the building can be photographed from the surrounding public streets and squares.

name: St Paul's Pro-Cathedral
label: St Paul's Anglican
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Tigné Point' (1 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Tigné Point Beach' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/31233248: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Saint Paul's Anglican Cathedral' (79 m across).
notes: Neoclassical Anglican church with a tall spire.

text.description:
St Paul's Pro-Cathedral is the Anglican church of Valletta, and its slim spire is one of the easiest landmarks to pick out on the skyline. The church was commissioned by Dowager Queen Adelaide, who found that Anglicans on the island had nowhere of their own to worship. It was designed by William Scamp and built between 1839 and 1844 on the site of the old Auberge d'Allemagne. It is built of Maltese limestone in a neo-classical style, and the spire rises over 60 metres. A restoration of the building and steeple was completed in 2024.

The classic way to photograph it is from across the water at Tigné Point, on the Sliema side. From there the spire stands beside the Carmelite dome, with Valletta's sandstone walls spread out below. The best light comes in the hour before sunset, when the stone warms up, and the view carries on into blue hour. Tigné Point is a different, more distant viewpoint across the harbour, so check the map to see where you are. Use a little zoom to bring the spire and dome closer, and keep some water and sky in the frame so the skyline has room.

If you want a closer look at the church's neo-classical front and tall spire, Independence Square in Valletta is the alternative viewpoint.
text.geographic_location: St Paul's Pro-Cathedral stands in Independence Square in the middle of Valletta. The classic view of it is from Tigné Point, at the tip of Sliema, looking south across Marsamxett Harbour.
text.directions_text: For the classic view, head for Tigné Point, the last tip of Sliema on the far side of the harbour from Valletta. From the Tigné Point terrace, face south across the water and look for the spire beside the Carmelite dome. The church itself is in Independence Square, inside Valletta. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole skyline. Then switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the spire and the Carmelite dome closer together. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of sky and harbour, because the church will look very small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Tigné Point (Sliema side, across the harbour from Valletta (the last tip of Sliema)). Valletta's skyline at blue hour with St Paul's spire and the Carmelite dome side by side across the water. Tigné Point, on the Sliema side across the harbour from Valletta, is the classic viewpoint for the skyline with St Paul's spire and the Carmelite dome side by side across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the skyline on the lower third, with water at the bottom and sky above. Keep the spire and the dome both in the frame so they read as a pair. For a different angle, try Independence Square in Valletta, where the church's neo-classical front and tall spire stand against the balconied facades behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sunlit stonework to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky keeps its colour and the walls don't wash out. At blue hour, switch on night mode and brace your elbows on the railing or a wall to keep the shot sharp. Check the spire is upright in the frame before you press the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: About one hour before sunset, when the low, soft light warms Valletta's sandstone. Stay on into blue hour for the skyline with its lights coming on.

text.access_note: The Tigné Point viewpoint is an open public terrace, but check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside the church, as photography indoors may need a donation.

name: Auberge d'Aragon
label: Auberge d'Aragon
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Misraħ Indipendenza' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Misraħ Indipendenza' (way/247680422): middle (57 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/298475100: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Auberge of Aragon' (104 m across).
notes: Early Baroque-style palace of the Knights.

text.description: The Auberge d'Aragon is a low, plain limestone building that rewards a calm, straight-on photo. It was built from 1571 to house knights of the Order of Saint John from Aragon, Navarre and Catalonia, and the architect was Girolamo Cassar. It is the only auberge in Valletta that still has its original Mannerist design. That is why it looks so restrained: a single storey, a main doorway with three windows either side, rusticated corners and a continuous cornice along the roofline. The one big change is the Doric portico over the doorway, added around 1842 when the building was known as Gibraltar House. Later it served as the Office of the Prime Minister, and since 2020 it has housed the Ministry for Justice. It started out painted red ochre, and traces of that paint can still be seen at the back. It photographs well because the open square in front gives you the whole façade without anything in the way. Stand back far enough to fit the full width, and use the portico as your centrepiece. Keep your phone level so the cornice runs straight across the frame. The façade is not perfectly symmetrical, so don't worry if your composition is slightly off-centre. For a second angle, walk to Archbishop Street for a closer, lower view of the doorway, with the building filling the frame.
text.geographic_location: In the city of Valletta, on the square called Misraħ Indipendenza, right beside the Church of Our Lady of Pilar. The building's address is on Archbishop Street.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed for this spot, so simply head to Misraħ Indipendenza in Valletta. The auberge lies to the north-east of it, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full single-storey front. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are tight against the building, for example on Archbishop Street. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the portico, the cornice or the rusticated corners.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Misraħ Indipendenza (the piazza in front of the main façade). The full single-storey limestone front of the auberge with its later neoclassical portico, framed by the open square. From here the auberge is to the north-east, and you see the full limestone front with its later neoclassical portico, framed by the open square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the cornice up with a horizontal line so the building doesn't tilt. Put the portico and doorway near the middle and leave a little space on each side to show the full width. For a different view, try Archbishop Street for a closer, lower-angle shot of the doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the limestone keeps its detail. Keep the phone upright and level to avoid slanting walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually suits pale limestone better than harsh midday sun. Early in the day the square is likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed from the square and street, but the building is a working government office and is not generally open to the public. Interior photography is allowed only during select events, so plan to stay outside; if you fly a drone, check the local restrictions first.
